source_quality.notes: Printed footer runs page N of 20 and sits two render pages behind the printed number. Equations (2) to (14) and Figures 3, 4, 13 and 15 were read from review proxies; equation (1) and the definition of D rest on the text layer.

task_reconstruction.summary: Build an evacuation plan for a crowded museum that also flags bottlenecks, admits responders, and survives a change such as a fire in one room.

section_map.summary: Summary states the three parts and the two run times.
1.1 credits two pedestrian models and asks for a whole-to-local view.
1.2 lists five stated objectives and three implicit ones.
1.3 lays out four steps and a flow chart.
Sections 2 and 3 give five bare assumptions and a symbol table.
4.1 adopts the linear speed law and rejects it for high density.
4.2 builds the stable evacuation speed from front and side crowding.
5.1 and 5.2 turn the building into a graph and four matrices.
5.3 renames the goal as maximum flow and describes the dynamic loop.
Section 6 runs a synthetic building and classifies three bottlenecks.
Section 7 runs the Louvre and reads the exit-flow curve.
Section 8 gives the staff six steps.
Section 9 tests a five percent density error and lists strengths and limits.

contributions.summary: A stable evacuation speed mixing front crowding, side crowding and personnel traits, with three density regimes.
Two virtual nodes that cut many rooms and many exits down to one source and one sink.
A dynamic loop that rebuilds the maximum flow at every time step from the current density.
Flow margin, maximum flow minus actual flow, used to locate bottlenecks.

dependency_graph.via: their sum is the graph the algorithm reads

assumptions.summary: Signs are clear enough and most people are rational enough to follow them.
No stampedes, no counter-flow, and the main doors are of moderate size.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The test building draws room counts at random between 100 and 200 and sets three exit capacities at 40, 35 and 30 persons per second.
The Louvre is split into five floors, each a plane node map, with stairs as the links between floors, and people placed by room size.

models.summary: Nelson-Mowrer linear speed, k = 1 on stairs and k = 1.4 in corridors.
Stable evacuation speed from a force balance, integrated and weighted.
Dynamic maximum flow on the summed matrix, recomputed each time step.

verification.summary: A synthetic building of 770 people is reported solved in 0.457 seconds, with no recorded evacuation to compare against.
A five percent error in flow density leaves both curves overlapping until the final drop.

results_trace.summary: Louvre run: 36.15 seconds of compute for 6700 people at a 0.1 second step, total evacuation 288.7 seconds.
Widening the limiting channel cuts the test evacuation to about 43.2 seconds.
Exit flow starts near 140 persons per second, steps down to about 118, holds to roughly 250 seconds, and is gone by about 290 seconds.

writing_logic.summary: The summary names the job, concedes the difficulty, then gives the method in three parts and the numbers last.
Each speed model is closed by the case it cannot handle, which opens the next one.
Bottlenecks are counted and named before any one of them is analysed.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 3 draws rooms inside a box with a source node and a sink node, and the prose count of rooms disagrees with the nodes drawn.
Figure 4 shows the overall matrix as a block: initial strip on top, export strip on the right, core in the middle.
Figure 6 gives the flow at 15, 35 and 40 seconds and is read as an ordered plan.
Figure 7 contrasts the exit flow with its margin to show the supply shortfall.
Figure 12 shows the Louvre flow at 50, 120, 190 and 250 seconds, four lines meeting at the sink.
Figure 13 plots exit flow against time, falling in steps to near zero by about 290 seconds.
Figure 14 maps the margin at four times, red for fully loaded and blue for spare capacity.
Figure 15 overlays the original and the plus or minus five percent curves, separating only at the final drop.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A judge checking the five-minute claim can read it straight off the exit-flow curve.
The margin matrix is the device that makes a bottleneck visible rather than asserted.

weaknesses.summary: Equation (2) prints a minus on the left, so the force the prose calls damping would speed the person up.
The appendix code implements the linear law for both channel types and never the stable evacuation speed, and the emergency branch is commented out.
The product of two persons-per-metre densities is set equal to a persons-per-square-metre congestion.

independent_extensions.summary: The same reduction, two virtual nodes around a room graph, would transfer to any building whose exits can be metered.

unresolved_questions: What quantity is the a that the paper substitutes into equation (1)?
What values do alpha, beta, gamma, lambda_j and v_m take?
How can rho_1 times rho_2, in persons squared per square metre, equal D in persons per square metre?
Why does the summary say 6700 people and section 7.2 say about 7000?
Why does the prose take stair k as 1 while the code uses 1.08?
